meta.title: 10-Day Coding & System Design Comeback
meta.subtitle: Rebuild the muscle — competent and calm, not frozen.

rules.title: No AI, no autocomplete, no copilot — for all 10 days of practice.
rules.body: Plain editor or the LeetCode box. Type every character yourself. This feels awful for 2 days, then your recall comes back. The discomfort IS the muscle rebuilding.

rules.title: The 5-minute think rule.
rules.body: Before writing any code, spend 5 minutes restating the problem, an example, and your approach out loud. Coding before you have a plan is what causes freezing.

rules.title: The re-solve rule (most important).
rules.body: If stuck 25–30 min, read the solution — then CLOSE it and re-solve from a blank screen. Reading solutions feels productive but builds nothing. Re-solving from blank rebuilds recall.

rules.title: Talk while you code.
rules.body: Narrate your thinking out loud, even alone. Interviews are spoken — you must practice coding and explaining at the same time. This also fixes the 'mind wandering' problem.

rules.title: One pattern at a time.
rules.body: Don't jump around. Finish a pattern's problems before the next. Jumping around is how you feel busy but retain nothing.

rules.title: Track a tiny log.
rules.body: Each day write: problems solved, which I failed, which pattern. Re-attempt failed ones 2 days later. This single habit beats doing 2× the volume.

rules.title: Stop on time. Sleep.
rules.body: A tired brain doesn't encode memory. 4–6 focused hours beats 9 scattered ones. Protect sleep — it's when the learning consolidates.

dailyStructure.body: Warm up by re-solving 1 problem from yesterday (builds confidence), then 4–6 new problems on the day's pattern. Easy first, then medium.
Learn the day's concept (read + take notes in your own words), then connect it to PRISM/Tempo — 'where did I use this in real life?'
Update your log — solved / failed / pattern. Note one thing that clicked and one that didn't.

coding.guidance: Goal today is momentum — solve things you CAN do, rebuild the habit of finishing.

systemDesign.concepts: client → server → database. What an API is. HTTP verbs, status codes.
systemDesign.anchor: PRISM REST controllers — every endpoint maps a domain action to an HTTP verb + status code. You've lived this.

tasks.label: Read + notes in own words: client → server → DB, API, HTTP verbs, status code semantics
Write 1 paragraph: how PRISM maps domain errors → 409 / 422 / 404 via @RestControllerAdvice

wrapup.label: Log: solved / failed / pattern. Note one thing that clicked + one that didn't.

days.title: Basics continued — two pointers + hashmap patterns

coding.guidance: Pattern recognition: 'sorted array' or 'pair that sums to X' → think two pointers.

tasks.label: Re-solve 1 failed problem from Day 1, from blank

systemDesign.concepts: SQL vs NoSQL by access pattern. Indexing, primary keys, partitioning.
systemDesign.anchor: PRISM's Postgres partition-by-status (assets_active / assets_inactive / assets_default), composite PK (asset_id, status), deferred-cascade FK from asset_config. Tempo Runtime uses Cassandra because the access pattern is single-key (tenant, channel, pageType).

tasks.label: Read + notes: when SQL, when NoSQL, indexes (B-tree, partial, composite, GIN)
Write 1 paragraph: why PRISM is list-partitioned on status — what the composite PK and deferred-cascade FK actually solve

coding.guidance: Pattern: 'longest/shortest subarray with condition' → sliding window. 'Matching pairs / most recent' → stack.

systemDesign.concepts: Cache hit/miss, TTL, eviction (LRU/LFU), write-through vs write-back vs cache-aside.
systemDesign.anchor: Tempo Runtime's 3-tier cache: Ristretto L1 (in-process LFU, µs) → Meghacache L2 (18 nodes, single-digit ms) → Cassandra origin (low-tens ms). Cache-aside with TTL + Kafka-driven invalidation on publish.

tasks.label: Read + notes: cache-aside vs write-through vs write-behind; LRU = doubly linked list + hashmap
Write 1 paragraph: why Tempo Runtime has 3 tiers and how invalidation flows through Kafka on publish

coding.guidance: Linked list trick: draw the pointers on paper before coding. Always.

tasks.label: Re-attempt a Day 2–3 failure from blank

systemDesign.concepts: Horizontal vs vertical scaling, load balancer, statelessness, session affinity vs JWT.
systemDesign.anchor: Tempo Service runs active-active across useast4 / uscentral / EDC on GKE. Stateless pods, GSLB routes the user to the nearest region. HA = no SPOF + tested restore.

tasks.label: Read + notes: horizontal vs vertical, stateless services, LB types (L4 vs L7), session strategies
Write 1 paragraph: how Tempo Service stays stateless across 3 regions and what graceful shutdown gives you

coding.guidance: Recursion template: base case first, then recurse on children, then combine. BFS = queue; DFS = recursion or stack. Memorise both templates.

systemDesign.concepts: Async processing, pub/sub, Kafka, decoupling producers/consumers, the dual-write problem.
systemDesign.anchor: PRISM Forklift transactional outbox: outbox row written inside the same DB transaction as the entity mutation; drainer publishes to Kafka after commit. At-least-once delivery + idempotent downstream consumers (Pronto, IronBank, asset-discovery, P13N) = effectively exactly-once effect. THIS IS YOUR SIGNATURE STORY — rehearse it.

tasks.label: Read + notes: dual-write problem, transactional outbox pattern, at-least-once delivery, idempotent consumers
Write the 90-second Forklift outbox story end-to-end. Rehearse out loud, recorded.
Bonus: PRISM Message Hierarchy is a tree (M0 parent + variants). Note how state machine traversal on the tree drives P13N decisions.

coding.guidance: Pattern: 'sorted' + 'find/optimise' → binary search. Watch the mid overflow + boundary conditions.

tasks.label: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST
Kth Smallest Element in a BST
Re-solve a tree problem from Day 5, from blank

systemDesign.concepts: Replication, consistency vs availability (CAP), idempotency, retries with backoff + jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads.
systemDesign.anchor: Outbox + idempotent consumers from Day 5. Cassandra LOCAL_QUORUM writes + LOCAL_ONE reads on Tempo Runtime (writes durable across the DC, reads fast — freshness comes from Kafka invalidation, not from strong-read consistency). Resilience4j per-downstream breaker + thread pool in the Tempo V3 BFF.

tasks.label: Read + notes: CAP, eventual consistency, idempotency, exponential backoff + jitter, circuit breaker, bulkhead
Write 1 paragraph: why Tempo Runtime picks LOCAL_QUORUM writes / LOCAL_ONE reads — what tradeoff that's making

coding.guidance: DP intro only — don't rabbit-hole. Learn the '1D memo' shape, that's enough for now. Heap = priority queue; 'top K' / 'Kth' → heap.

systemDesign.topic: Full Design Framework — practice on URL shortener
systemDesign.concepts: The 6-step framework: clarify → estimate → API → high-level → deep-dive 1–2 → bottlenecks & tradeoffs.
systemDesign.anchor: URL shortener walkthrough: pre-generated counter + base62 (3.5T short codes in 7 chars), KV store (Redis + DynamoDB), cache the redirects, async analytics via Kafka. Compare to Tempo's authoring/delivery split — same shape, different access patterns.

tasks.label: Memorise the 6 steps cold — recite all 6 with no prompt
Design URL shortener out loud, the full 6-step walk, recorded

coding.guidance: Pick 4 random medium problems across patterns. 30 min each, timed, NO solution peeking until time's up. Narrate out loud the whole time. Then review: which patterns did you recognise fast? Which froze you?

tasks.label: Medium problem #1 (30 min timed, narrated, no peeking)
Review: patterns recognised fast vs froze on. Log them.

systemDesign.topic: Practice design out loud — rate limiter, news feed
systemDesign.concepts: Two more real designs to walk through. Rate limiter: token bucket in Redis, key by user/IP/tenant, 429 with Retry-After. News feed: fan-out-on-write vs fan-out-on-read, when each.
systemDesign.anchor: Token bucket → Redis INCR + EXPIRE → 429. You used this exact shape on Tempo V3 BFF (60 req/min per user). News feed = fan-out tradeoff is the same shape as Tempo's authoring/delivery split.

tasks.label: Design a rate limiter, full 6-step framework out loud, recorded
Design a news feed, full 6-step framework out loud, recorded
Listen back to recordings — flag wandering / rambling moments

wrapup.label: Log: which patterns were sticky, which weren't

coding.guidance: Redo the patterns that froze you on Day 8. 5–6 problems, timed. Confidence check: you've now solved ~40 problems — that's the proof, not a feeling.

tasks.label: Re-solve 3 hardest failures of the plan, from blank — #1

systemDesign.topic: Design Tempo / PRISM — your secret weapon
systemDesign.concepts: Take 'design a content management + delivery platform' as a real prompt. You've built it. Speak with operating authority, not theory.
systemDesign.anchor: Authoring write-path (Tempo Service + PRISM) → Kafka outbox → Sync Service → Cassandra delivery (Tempo Runtime). 38 tenants, ~27 TPS writes, 4K TPS reads, p95 35–45 ms. Multi-tenant by tenant ID at every layer. Canary by tenant group (TG1/TG2/TG3). Deep-dive: partitioned Postgres + composite PK + deferred-cascade FK; Cassandra schema partitioned by (tenant, channel, pageType); 3-tier cache.

tasks.label: Design Tempo/PRISM as if interview prompt — full 6-step framework, recorded
Rehearse the rapid-fire numbers cold: 150×, 38 tenants, 12k+ msgs, ~27 TPS, p95 250ms, $11/day, >92% trace propagation, 15 services in BFF

wrapup.label: Log: which numbers stuck, which I had to look up. Re-rehearse the misses.

days.title: Light review + rest — DO NOT CRAM

coding.guidance: Re-solve 5 problems you previously failed, from blank. If they go smoothly, you're ready. Re-read the pattern cheat list. Skim, don't grind. Stop early. Rest.

tasks.label: Skim the 11 patterns cheat list — name each one + when to use it, no answers from the doc

systemDesign.concepts: Re-read the 6-step framework and your PRISM anchors. Don't take new notes. Skim only.
systemDesign.anchor: Your unfair advantage: PRISM and Tempo are a real distributed system you built — CMS with authoring/delivery split, caching tiers, transactional outbox, partitioned databases, multi-region deployment. Most candidates invent these from theory. Speak from having operated them.

Prepare 2–3 questions to ask them at the end of the interview

framework.title: The 6-Step System Design Framework
framework.tagline: Use this exact order on EVERY design question. The order itself stops you from wandering — same fix as behavioural answers.

steps.title: Clarify requirements (3–5 min)
steps.body: Functional (what it does) + non-functional (scale, latency, consistency). Ask: how many users? reads vs writes? Don't design until you know the scale. Interviewers WANT you to ask.

steps.title: Estimate scale
steps.body: Rough numbers — QPS, storage, read/write ratio. Even ballpark shows you think about scale. Recipe: DAU × actions/day ÷ 86,400 = avg QPS, × 3 for peak, × bytes for storage.

steps.title: Define the API
steps.body: A few key endpoints with inputs/outputs. This grounds everything that follows.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.body: Draw the boxes: client → load balancer → service(s) → cache → database → queue. Talk through one request's path end to end.

steps.title: Deep-dive 1–2 components
steps.body: Pick the interesting parts — the data model, the caching strategy, how you keep things in sync. THIS is where your PRISM / outbox / partitioning knowledge shines. Steer toward what you've operated.

steps.title: Address bottlenecks & tradeoffs
steps.body: Where does it break at scale? Consistency vs availability? Single points of failure? Naming tradeoffs out loud is what separates senior from junior.

framework.advantage: PRISM and Tempo are a real distributed system you built — a CMS with authoring/delivery split, caching tiers, a transactional outbox, partitioned databases, and multi-region deployment. Most candidates invent these from theory. You can speak from having operated them. In the deep-dive step, steer toward what you know.
